appraisal_events.evidence: The duchesse de Guermantes calls him 'mon plus vieil ami,' says 'vous n'avez pour ainsi dire pas changé' and 'vous restez toujours jeune,' then delivers what the narrator calls 'le dernier coup' about surviving sons killed in war; a nephew of the prince calls him 'un vieux Parisien'; young Létourville's letter signs off 'votre petit ami,' the very phrase the narrator once used for men thirty years his senior.
appraisal_events.explanation: Several speakers in quick succession ('coup sur coup,' 'les trompettes du Jugement') unwittingly reveal to the narrator that he is now perceived as old, with the duchesse's remarks the most extended and explicitly painful instance of this collective revelation.

appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch now wears flattened, cosmetic-slicked hair, an English 'chic,' and a monocle that 'dispensait' his face of the human duties of expressing beauty or spirit; his nose is disguised and his manner has taken on 'la docte fatigue des vieillards aimables,' so that the narrator has trouble recognizing him at all.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator describes Bloch's aged, self-fashioned appearance with satirical detail, presenting his artificial reinvention as a loss of his former youthful vitality.

status_effects.explanation: The cumulative, ostensibly affectionate remarks about his age devastate the narrator, forcing an unwelcome recognition of his own aging that he explicitly likens to the trumpets of Judgment.

He is repeatedly placed in the category of the old by younger speakers (addressed as 'vieux Parisien,' called 'petit ami' by a young sous-lieutenant), excluding him from the youthful camaraderie he still imagines himself part of.
Bloch's artificial self-transformation and visible aging are described critically, diminishing him relative to the vital, unaffected youth the narrator remembers.

ambiguities: The 'trumpets of judgment' passage attributes the aging-revelation to several distinct speakers (the duchesse, an unnamed nephew of the prince, Létourville, an unnamed well-wisher); the annotation treats this as one collective movement rather than crediting a single named source, though the duchesse's words are the most extensively quoted instance.
Létourville does not appear on the reference sheet and is recorded as unresolved, though he is clearly a distinct named character within this passage.
